title: The owl: a most distinctive bird

paragraphs.text: People most often encounter owls at night, sometimes as a mysterious, and perhaps unpleasant, cry in the darkness. Many cultures have believed that owls bring bad luck, and even today, owls are sometimes hunted because of such fears. Yet the ancient Greeks perceived owls more positively, as representations of wisdom. The owl portrayed on Greek coins from 2,000 years ago represents a real species. Athene noctua, also known as the little owl of Athena, still seen in the Mediterranean region today.

Owls are hunters, and many of their remarkable characteristics developed for this reason. They have large claws and legs, a fact that some may not know, in addition to wing feathers designed for silent flight, and highly sensitive eyes and ears. Contrary to popular myth, they can see in daylight and in some species, better than humans. Unlike most birds, both of their large, round eyes face forward, and can’t shift from side to side. However, this is compensated for by owls’ ability to rotate their head around 270 degrees. One type of owl even has eye-like markings on the back of its head to confuse predators.

Hearing is even more important to owls than seeing. In some owls, one ear is larger and located higher on the head, which helps them catch prey hidden in total darkness or under the snow. Tiny variances in when noises reach the owl’s ears, as little as 30 millionths of a second, allow the owl to pinpoint the other animal’s exact location.

There are over 200 species of owl but the number continues to change. For one thing, vulnerable species are becoming extinct. Tropical owls, for example, are at risk due to deforestation to make way for agriculture. And such species that are limited to a single island, for instance in Indonesia or the Philippines, are particularly vulnerable to invasive predators like rats and snakes On the other hand, other owl species are still being discovered. One reason is that it has become easier for researchers to capture the sounds of owls in the wild since the arrival of the portable digital recorder in the 1990s. Owls are intensely territorial, so when a male owl hears a rival invade his territory, he attacks. Researchers using speakers can pose as an intruder and quickly bring an angry male into view, and capture its calls.

Techniques like this have changed the way owls are classified by researchers. The use of sound recordings has shown that owls of similar appearance, once considered the same species, may sound different. Indeed, owl courtship is primarily vocal, rather than visual: A female owl will not mate with a male unless he gives the right vocal cues. Now, similar-looking populations with distinct vocal calls are classified as separate species. In addition, some new species have been identified by analyzing their genes, though this is much more expensive and difficult than using sound.

It should be remembered that very little is known about many of these new species, since they inhabit areas of deep wilderness. Indeed, there are at least 20 species worldwide for which there are no photographs. Some newly-found species may become extinct before we learn how they live, and others may be reclassified as subspecies in the future.

Today, owls have adapted themselves to many different environments, including cities. For instance, barn owls have nested in abandoned buildings and water tanks atop buildings in New York. Also, during cold weather, the impressively beautiful snowy owl flies south to spend the winter in the Now York area. The attention this brings has sometimes led to conflict between crowds of people trying to take pictures of the owls and local bird enthusiasts attempting to protect the birds’ privacy. In one populous suburb near Philadelphia, 237 owls were found in an area 25 kilometers across. One of the largest owls, the Eurasian eagle owl, is commonly found in densely populated parts of western Europe, since it doesn’t fear humans. There are plenty of rodents and small birds to eat in modern cities for owls that don’t mind human company.

One common feature of modern human settlements, electrical power lines, has obvious dangers for owls. However, since the areas around power lines are cleared of trees, this provides open terrain that allows owls to more easily. Identify prey, such as mice and other small animals. And an owl can sit on a power line or pole and survey the surrounding ground.

Vehicles, however, pose clear risks. Many owls use highways and nearby areas for hunting, flying in close to the ground when they spot their prey. Since they have frontally situated eyes, an owl flying across a road may be unaware of oncoming vehicles and be struck.

Some more fragile owl species struggle to survive other challenges to their habitats. The little owl of Athena has become much rarer in the Mediterranean area, probably because widespread use of pesticides has eliminated many of the large bugs it eats. And of course, nature itself often presents challenges. In the 1980s, the US government successfully protected the habitat of the spotted owl from extensive tree cutting by the logging industry. Yet today the spotted owl remains under a different threat: The slightly larger barred owl is increasingly taking over its territory.
